bib.title: Can Agents Infer Environment from Interaction? Evidence from Agentic Automata Learning

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Can Agents Infer Environment from Interaction? Evidence from Agentic Automata Learning" (arXiv 2606.16576v2, 27 Sep 2026). Reef Menaged, Gili Lior, Gabriel Stanovsky (Hebrew University of Jerusalem), Shauli Ravfogel (NYU), Roee Aharoni (Google Research). Preprint, "Under review at ICLR 2027". Ledger lists an older title, "Can LLM Agents Infer World Models?"; the ledger row is key 2606.16576, status downloaded.

COVERAGE: 62,725 chars extracted (pypdf). I read 0-41,000 and 44,000-62,725. I skipped about 3,000 chars at 41,000-44,000, which is mid-reference-list (Li through Yang). That includes the ICML 2018 Weiss et al. entry, so the reference list was only skimmed. All of the body, the conclusion and the Appendix A and B text were read. Figures 3-9 are plots, and I read only their extracted axis text and captions, not the images. Appendix A.7 and B hold only figures with captions, and Table 2 is in A.5.

CORE CLAIM: A hidden DFA is a procedurally generated, size-controlled testbed for whether tool-calling LLM agents can infer a hidden environment from queries. Frontier models fall off sharply as the DFA grows, and an explicit state-tracking scaffold helps the stronger models but not a smaller one. Models name and can code L*, yet do not execute it reliably. In the authors' words, "knowing how to solve a task is not sufficient".

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Success falls with DFA size, and the best figure at 8-9 states is low.
 number: 30.0% stateless, 57.5% stateful
 setup: 3 models (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3.8 Flash), reasoning high. 160 instances in 4 state buckets, n=40 per bucket. The grader is deterministic: an equivalence query within budget returns ⊤. The 95% CI is bootstrapped (100,000 resamples). One run per instance as far as I can tell (see Limits).
 quote: "For automata with 8 or 9 states, the highest success rate is 57.5% under the stateful scaffold and 30.0% under the stateless scaffold."
 where: Sec 5, p6
2. Efficiency gap to classic learners.
 number: about 23.5% more tool calls than TTT
 setup: 8-9 states, successful runs only, best model-scaffold pair (Gemini 3.1 Pro, stateful). The metric is ΔTool Calls against min(L*, TTT).
 quote: "uses approximately 23.5% more tool calls than TTT."
 where: p7
3. Models know L* but do not execute it.
 number: 31%
 setup: In a separate OpenHands run with a coding tool and no internet, all models wrote L*. In the interaction runs, no instance reproduced the L* query sequence. The 31% is the share of runs where DeepSeek-v4-Pro with the stateful scaffold keeps equivalence queries ≤ number of states and hypothesis size monotone. The OpenHands run has no numbers.
 quote: "Even the combination closest to classic behavior, DeepSeek-v4-Pro with a stateful scaffold, satisfies both properties in only 31% of runs."
 where: p7
4. The state scaffold helps strong models and hurts the small one.
 number: invalid tool calls for Flash rose from 0.2% to 8.7%. Gemini 3.1 Pro cost per run fell from $10 to $3.25.
 setup: stateful means ReAct-style fields (goal, working memory, thought) carried forward. Table 2 gives the invalid-call rates.
 quote: "increase in its invalid tool-call rate from 0.2% to 8.7% when state tracking is added." / "average cost per run decreases from $10 to $3.25."
 where: p7, p9, A.5
5. Failure taxonomy: planning vs reasoning, graded by classic passive learners (RPNI, EDSM, Blue-Fringe).
 number: none (shares are plotted in Fig 4b, not stated in the text)
 setup: a planning failure is when no passive learner recovers the DFA from the model's collected evidence. A reasoning failure is when one can, but the model did not.
 quote: "A planning failure occurs when the model fails and none of the classic passive learning algorithms, RPNI, EDSM, or Blue-Fringe, introduced in Section 2.2, can infer the hidden DFA from the observations accumulated by the model"
 where: p8
6. Non-informative queries rise as the interaction gets longer, and state tracking reduces but does not remove them.
 number: none (curves only)
 setup: a membership query is non-informative if the word was queried before. An equivalence query is non-informative if it duplicates a hypothesis or contradicts known evidence.
 quote: "the rate of non-informative queries increases as interactions grow longer"
 where: p8
7. The budget matters a lot.
 number: DeepSeek 3.1% to 55.6%; Gemini 3.1 Pro 54.4% at 125% and 70.6% at 200%
 setup: budget = 100-200% of min(L*, TTT) queries, stateless (Fig 5 legend). The default budget is 2x.
 quote: "DeepSeek-v4-Pro improves from 3.1% at 100% to 55.6% at 200%" / "Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview reaches 54.4% success already at 125% of the baseline budget ... reaching 70.6% at 200%."
 where: p9
8. Cost.
 number: up to about 16M tokens, 20 hours and $50 per run; $3000 total.
 quote: "reaching up to about 16 million tokens, 20 hours, and $50 per run. Overall, the total monetary cost of the full experimental suite was $3000."
 where: p8-9
9. Failures are not caused by context overflow.
 number: none
 setup: no trajectory crosses the context limit (Fig 8). The limits are 1M/1.05M tokens.
 quote: "Since no trajectory crosses this line, the observed failures cannot be attributed to exceeding the available context window."
 where: A.7, p19

DESIGN DETAILS worth citing
- The query budget is 2x the better of L*/TTT, so "a correct solution exists within the allocated query budget."
- Instances come from Boltzmann sampling of minimal DFAs over a binary alphabet.
- The counterexample is a short word chosen deterministically from lengths k_min..k_min+3.
- Malformed calls are discarded and not counted against the budget.
- Seeds 1-20 for each size 2-9.
- The appendix also defines Best Hypothesis Similarity, over all words up to length 200 via a product-DFA dynamic programme. This is a graded, partial-credit complement to binary success.

LIMITS
Stated: the DFAs are simpler than real environments. The alphabet is fixed at binary. Evaluation is expensive. Future work covers nondeterministic or stochastic environments. OpenAI and Claude models were left out for cost: "We did not include OpenAI or Claude models because evaluating their high-reasoning configurations at the same scale would have substantially increased the total API cost."
Unstated:
- Only three models, two of them from one vendor.
- No stated repeats per instance, so there is no pass@k or pass^k and no run-to-run variance. The "n=40 runs" per bucket equals the instances.
- The CI is over instances only.
- The ΔTool Calls average covers successful runs only, so it is biased toward easy cases.
- The failure split (planning vs reasoning) depends on the passive learners' power, and the shares are not given as numbers in the text.
- The model dates are in the future relative to my own knowledge: DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Gemini 3.8 Flash. I report them as printed.
- The stateful and stateless prompts differ in more than state (the stateless prompt forbids any text output), so the gain is partly "allowed to think visibly". The paper does not separate the two.
- "Gemini 3.8 Flash" is dated Sept 2026 in the references, the same month as the runs.
- No human baseline.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES
- The abstract and intro say "highest success rate is only 30.0%" for 8-9 states. The intro then says "raising the highest success rate in this setting to 57.5%". Fine, but the abstract's "drops sharply" gives no number.
- Figure 3 says n=40 "runs" per bucket, while the appendix says 20 seeds per size, 2 sizes per bucket (40 instances). Consistent only if there is one run per instance.
- The text says the stateful scaffold "reduces cost across models", but Flash's invalid-call rate rose, and no Flash cost figure is given.
- The Fig 5 budget percentages (DeepSeek 55.6%, Gemini 70.6% at 200%) are overall, stateless, and differ from the 8-9-state figures. They are not directly comparable to the headline 30.0%.
- The method text says a "stateful DeepSeek" example in Fig 2. Table 1's Gemini solves with equivalence queries only, a different style, which illustrates that the success metric ignores strategy.
- The abstract says models "can implement and execute them when given access to a coding environment", but no success numbers for that arm are reported. This is a weak spot.

BUILDS ON: Angluin 1987/1988/1990 (L*, query learning); Isberner, Howar and Steffen 2014 (TTT); Isberner 2015 (thesis); Bassino and Nicaud 2007 (Boltzmann DFA sampling); Oncina and Garcia 1992, Lang et al. 1998 (RPNI, EDSM, Blue-Fringe); Yao et al. 2023 (ReAct); Rozanov and Rei 2025 (state tracking); OpenHands (Wang et al. 2025); Yang et al. 2025 (AQA-Bench); Vafa et al. 2024; AgencyBench (Li et al. 2026) for the size justification; Hesterberg 2015 (bootstrap).

CODE: none worth keeping. The metric is ΔTool Calls = mean over successful runs of (T_M − min{T_L*, T_TTT}). The tool names are `is_word_in_language` and `evaluate_dfa_candidate` (A.1).

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Fig 3 (p7), success rate by DFA-size bucket for stateful vs stateless across 3 models, with bootstrap CIs. It shows controlled difficulty scaling in a single plot. Alternatively Fig 2 (p5), the stateless vs stateful scaffold with an L* observation table in working memory. Fig 4b splits planning from reasoning failures. Table 1 (p3) shows Gemini solving with equivalence queries only, against L* and TTT.

NOTE FIT: The target note 06-evaluating-agents.md has these sections: Outcome and trajectory; Grade the outcome by state; Scoring tool calls; Evaluate the components, then the whole; Non-determinism: run every task k times; Efficiency metrics (with "Convergence in practice" and the failure-end-reason paragraphs on AgentBench, AutoLab, Terminal-Bench, OAT); Agent-specific suites; Multi-turn evaluation; Environment hygiene; Pitfalls. I found no DFA or automata mention in any note under 08-eval/notes/.
- Best-fit section: "Efficiency metrics", right after the paragraphs on log-why-runs-end and failure localisation. This paper contributes (a) a cost-in-queries metric measured against a provable optimal baseline, (b) a failure classification by checking whether the gathered evidence sufficed, and (c) non-informative-query rate over time.
- It also links to "Convergence in practice" (optimal steps divided by actual steps), since ΔTool Calls against L*/TTT is the same idea with a proven optimum.
- A second, lighter fit is "Environment hygiene" or "Agent-specific suites" for procedural generation, budget set to 2x the optimum, and a solvability guarantee.
- The note currently lacks: a task with a provable-optimum baseline, size-controlled difficulty, and a way to tell "did not gather the evidence" from "gathered it but did not use it".
- Another note, 03-eval-datasets.md (procedurally generated, size-controlled instances), is a plausible secondary home for the generation point only. Chapter 12-failure-modes.md is less apt.
- The ledger row is key 2606.16576 with `"note": "generative-ai/08-eval/notes/06-evaluating-agents.md"`.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. No extraction faults beyond spacing (words run together in the title and figure text). The 41,000-44,000 gap is references only. The figures were not rendered, so the Fig 4b shares and the Fig 5/9 values are unread. I cannot verify the model names beyond the paper's own statements.
